name: Ace of Cups
symbolism: A hand reaches out of a cloud holding a cup, from which water pours in five streams into a pool full of water lilies. A white dove descends over the vessel with a small disc in its beak, and tiny drops like falling petals float all around.
upright: The Ace of Cups speaks of a moment when feelings begin to flow more freely. It may be a new relationship, a renewed friendship or simply a gentler view of yourself. The card invites you to accept what comes without hurry and without judging. It is worth noticing what you would like to share with others today.
reversed: The reversed Ace may suggest that emotions are present but held inside, as if the vessel were covered. Sometimes this is a need for protection, sometimes weariness from giving. A good step is often to fill your own cup first.
reflection: Which feeling would like to be noticed by me today?
To whom or what can I show gratitude without expecting anything back?
advice: Open your heart. Let yourself feel and receive what is good: a new feeling or relationship may begin now.
adviceReversed: You are closing yourself off from emotions. Consider what you are afraid of, and give yourself permission to feel.

name: Two of Cups
symbolism: A young man and a young woman stand facing each other and exchange cups, as if making a promise. Above them floats a staff entwined with two serpents and crowned with a winged lion's head, and a peaceful house among hills can be seen in the background.
upright: The Two of Cups describes a bond based on a balance of giving and taking. It is not only about romance but about every meeting in which both sides feel seen. The card suggests that honesty and attentive listening can bring people closer than grand gestures. It is a good moment to appreciate the people with whom you share mutual respect.
reversed: Reversed, the card may draw attention to an unequal share of attention or to unspoken expectations. It can also signal that you first need to come to an understanding with yourself.
reflection: In which relationship do I feel truly listened to?
What do I need in order to give and receive in balance?
advice: Go for understanding. Reach out and look for reciprocity: there is good energy in the relationship right now.
adviceReversed: Something is missing in the relationship: balance or honesty. Talk about it before the distance grows.

name: Three of Cups
symbolism: Three women in colourful robes dance in a circle and raise their cups high. Ripe fruit, pumpkins and grapes lie at their feet, bringing to mind harvest time and feasting together.
upright: The Three of Cups is a reminder of the strength of community and of joy shared with others. It may encourage you to celebrate small successes or to get back in touch with friends. The card emphasises that support often comes in a light form: conversation, laughter, a shared meal. It is worth asking yourself where you feel part of something bigger.
reversed: The reversed Three may speak of having had too much company, or of feeling a little apart from the group. It can also be an invitation to celebrate quietly, at your own pace.
reflection: With whom would I like to share my latest good moment?
Where do I feel part of a community, and where only a guest?
advice: Meet the people who are on your side. Shared joy and support will help you with this matter.
adviceReversed: Too much company, or gossip, may get in the way. Choose whom you really trust.

name: Four of Cups
symbolism: A young man sits under a tree with his arms folded, looking at three cups standing on the grass in front of him. To one side a hand emerges from a cloud offering a fourth cup, which he does not seem to notice.
upright: The Four of Cups describes a state of withdrawal in which what is familiar no longer brings joy. Such a pause may be necessary in order to understand what you really want. The card gently suggests, though, that you look up now and then, because something new may be waiting beside you. You do not have to accept it straight away; it is enough to notice it.
reversed: Reversed, the card may mean slowly coming out of a rut and being more open to offers. It may also suggest that the withdrawal is lasting longer than you need.
reflection: What around me has stopped bringing me joy, and why?
Which offer might I have overlooked lately?
advice: You are being offered something but not noticing it. Look around: the opportunity may be closer than you think.
adviceReversed: You are coming out of apathy, and that is good. Now accept what you have been turning down until now.

name: Five of Cups
symbolism: A figure in a long black cloak stands bowed over three overturned cups from which liquid has spilled. Behind the figure stand two more full cups, and further off a river flows, crossed by a bridge leading to a house.
upright: The Five of Cups gives room for sadness over something that did not go as hoped. The card does not tell you to shake it off quickly; rather, it acknowledges that grief is a natural part of living through things. At the same time it is a reminder of the two cups still standing. When you are ready, you can turn round and see what you still have.
reversed: The reversed Five may signal that the process of coming to terms with the loss is already under way and more gentleness is appearing. Sometimes, though, it points to sadness hidden deep inside that needs to be expressed safely.
reflection: Which grief do I allow myself to feel, and which do I avoid?
What of value is still with me, despite what has spilled?
advice: Allow yourself to grieve, but do not stay there. Turn round: not everything has been lost.
adviceReversed: You are beginning to get back on your feet after the loss. Focus on what remains and take the first step forward.

name: Six of Cups
symbolism: In the courtyard of an old village a boy hands a girl a cup filled with white flowers. More vessels of flowers stand around them, and in the background a guard walks away, as if watching over this peaceful place.
upright: The Six of Cups calls up the warmth of memories and simple gestures of kindness. It may encourage you to get in touch with someone from the past, or to remember what used to make you happy. The card speaks of giving without calculation, as children do. It is worth checking which old joys could come back to life today in a new form.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to holding on too tightly to the past, or idealising what has gone. It can also encourage you to take what was good from old lessons and move on.
reflection: Which memory gives me a sense of warmth today?
Is there something from the past that I can now gently put aside?
advice: Reach for what was good in the past: simplicity, kindness, an old friendship. They may help you now.
adviceReversed: Do not live in your memories. What was will not come back in the same form: it is time to look ahead.

name: Seven of Cups
symbolism: A dark silhouette stands before seven cups floating in the clouds. Each holds something different: a head, a veiled glowing figure, a serpent, a castle, jewels, a wreath and a dragon, as if every vessel promised a different future.
upright: The Seven of Cups shows the richness of the imagination and the many paths you can dream up. It is a beautiful space, but an easy one to get lost in. The card invites you to tell apart what truly moves you from what merely glitters. One small, concrete step can help you check which dream has life in it.
reversed: The reversed Seven may mean that the fog is clearing and it is easier for you to choose. It may also point to being overloaded with options, when it is worth narrowing your field of view.
reflection: Which of my dreams is really mine, and which have I taken over from others?
Which one small step would help me test the possibility I have chosen?
advice: You have many possibilities, but not all of them are real. Choose one concrete option and separate dreams from plans.
adviceReversed: The fog is clearing and you can already see what matters. Now make the decision.

name: Eight of Cups
symbolism: A figure in a red cloak, leaning on a staff, walks away towards mountains and water under a night sky in which the moon has a human face. Behind the figure eight cups are left carefully arranged in two rows, with a clear gap in the top row.
upright: The Eight of Cups speaks of the moment when what has been built is no longer enough for the heart. It is not about failure but about a need for deeper meaning. The card may support a decision to walk away from a habit, a role or a belief that no longer serves you. Leaving can be a form of self-respect here.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to wavering: wanting change while being afraid to leave the familiar. It can also be a signal to look once more at what you are leaving before you set off.
reflection: What am I looking for that I cannot find where I am now?
What can I leave behind with gratitude rather than regret?
advice: Walk away from what no longer nourishes you. It takes courage, but you are going in search of something deeper.
adviceReversed: You are torn between leaving and staying. Check whether you are running away or really looking for something better.

name: Nine of Cups
symbolism: A contented man sits on a wooden bench with his arms folded and his head slightly raised. Behind him, on a curved table covered with blue cloth, stands an even row of nine cups.
upright: The Nine of Cups describes a feeling that things are good and your wishes have been met, at least in part. It is an invitation to allow yourself joy without guilt. The card is also a reminder that satisfaction tastes fuller when it is conscious, not just ticked off. Pause for a moment over what has already gone well.
reversed: The reversed Nine may point to a contentment that is superficial or depends on outward signs. Sometimes it suggests asking what you truly want, rather than what you are supposed to have.
reflection: What gives me real, quiet satisfaction?
Do I allow myself to enjoy what I have achieved?
advice: The answer is yes: your wish has a good chance of coming true. Enjoy it and appreciate what you already have.
adviceReversed: Outward contentment is not enough. Consider what you really want, not just what you are supposed to have.

name: Ten of Cups
symbolism: A couple stand with their arms round each other and raise their arms towards a rainbow, in whose arc ten cups shine. Beside them two children dance, and in the distance a small house can be seen by a river among green hills.
upright: The Ten of Cups speaks of a sense of emotional home: a place or people around whom you can be yourself. It need not be a family in the traditional sense, but any community built on care. The card encourages you to appreciate everyday harmony, even if it is not perfect. It is worth considering what you yourself bring to that shared peace.
reversed: Reversed, the card may draw attention to the gap between the picture of an ideal home and the reality. It can be an invitation to an honest conversation about what each of your loved ones needs.
reflection: Where, and with whom, do I feel truly at home?
What can I do today to bring more warmth to those around me?
advice: Go for closeness and harmony. What you are building with your loved ones matters most right now: look after it.
adviceReversed: Behind the picture of the ideal family or relationship there is tension. Talk honestly about your needs.

name: Page of Cups
symbolism: A young man in a tunic with a floral pattern stands at the seashore holding a cup from which a small fish is peeping. He looks at it with curiosity, as if holding a quiet conversation with it, and gentle waves roll behind him.
upright: The Page of Cups is an invitation to play with your own feelings and imagination. An unexpected idea, a dream or an impression worth writing down may appear. The card encourages openness and a little childlike naivety, in the best sense of the word. Not everything has to make sense straight away in order to be valuable.
reversed: The reversed Page may suggest that sensitivity is being held back for fear of judgement. It may also point to emotional unsteadiness, which a gentle structure to the day can help with.
reflection: Which idea or feeling has surprised me lately?
Where can I allow myself more creative play?
advice: Listen to your intuition and be open to emotional messages. A small, sensitive spark can turn into something.
adviceReversed: Emotional immaturity or oversensitivity is getting in the way. Do not take everything personally.

name: Knight of Cups
symbolism: A knight in armour with small wings on his helmet and heels rides slowly on a white horse, holding a cup before him like a gift. His horse steps calmly, and a river flows and gentle hills rise in the background.
upright: The Knight of Cups carries the energy of a heart that wants to act. It may mean an invitation, a gesture of affection or a creative project pursued with passion. The card emphasises the value of gentleness and sincerity in what you offer. It is worth checking, though, that your ideals also have ground under their feet.
reversed: The reversed Knight may point to too much daydreaming, or moods that change direction from day to day. It can also be a signal not to make promises before you feel they are realistic.
reflection: What would I like to offer someone from the bottom of my heart?
Are my ideals grounded in everyday life?
advice: Follow your heart: make the offer, express your feelings. Romance and sincerity are on your side right now.
adviceReversed: Do not get carried away by idealism. Check whether the promises are backed by actions.

name: Queen of Cups
symbolism: The queen sits on a throne set right at the water's edge, her feet almost touching the water. In her hands she holds a richly decorated, closed cup with angel-shaped handles and gazes at it thoughtfully; the throne is decorated with figures of sea children and shells.
upright: The Queen of Cups embodies a mature sensitivity that can feel compassion without losing itself. The card encourages you to trust your hunches and give yourself time to listen to what is happening inside. It may also point to a person around whom others feel safe. Your empathy is precious, especially when it includes you too.
reversed: Reversed, the card may mean taking on other people's emotions as your own, or losing your boundaries. It can be an invitation to look after your own inner waters first.
reflection: What is my intuition telling me today?
How can I support others without losing myself?
advice: Be guided by empathy, towards others and towards yourself. Your intuition is leading you well.
adviceReversed: You give others too much and yourself too little. Set healthy emotional boundaries.

name: King of Cups
symbolism: The king sits on a stone throne that seems to float on a rolling sea. In one hand he holds a cup, in the other a sceptre; around his neck he wears a fish-shaped pendant, and in the background a ship sails and a sea creature leaps from the water.
upright: The King of Cups shows that you can feel deeply and stay calm at the same time. It is the energy of someone who does not suppress emotions but understands them and handles them wisely. The card encourages gentle leadership and conversations conducted with kindness. Things may be stormy around you, and you can remain your own island.
reversed: The reversed King may point to emotions kept under too tight a control, looking for a way out. Sometimes it is a signal to allow yourself more honesty with yourself.
reflection: How do I react to the emotional waves around me?
In what way can I be a calm and kind support for someone?
advice: Stay calm and mature. Master your emotions without suppressing them: that is the key to a good decision.
adviceReversed: Emotions are getting the upper hand, or they are locked away. Find a safe way to express them.

name: Ace of Swords
symbolism: A hand emerges from a cloud gripping an upright sword whose blade pierces a crown. Sprigs of olive and palm hang from the crown, small sparks fall all around, and harsh rocky peaks stretch out below.
upright: The Ace of Swords brings a moment of clarity, when thoughts suddenly fall into a clear picture. It may be a new idea, an understanding of the situation, or a readiness to call things by their names. The card encourages you to be honest with yourself and to speak the truth thoughtfully. Clarity is a tool that serves best when it is joined with kindness.
reversed: The reversed Ace may point to thoughts circling without direction, or to a truth you do not yet want to hear. It can also be a signal to slow down before sharp words are spoken too quickly.
reflection: What has become clear to me lately?
How can I express my truth with respect for others?
advice: Speak the truth and think clearly. A breakthrough is close: one well-aimed decision will cut through the confusion.
adviceReversed: Your thoughts are tangled. Before you decide, gather the facts and separate them from your worries.

name: Two of Swords
symbolism: A woman in a white robe sits on a bench, blindfolded, holding two crossed swords against her chest. Behind her stretches water dotted with rocks, and a thin crescent moon can be seen in the sky.
upright: The Two of Swords describes a moment when a choice seems hard and the mind is looking for balance. The blindfold may mean a wish to cut yourself off from the chaos in order to hear your own voice. The card allows a moment of reflection, but reminds you that the stalemate need not last for ever. Sometimes it is enough to lift the blindfold and look at the facts.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to tension that is finally demanding a decision, or to an excess of information. It can also be a signal that you are already feeling ready to break the deadlock.
reflection: Which choice am I stopping in front of right now?
What do I need to know in order to feel more certain?
advice: You are avoiding a decision by covering your eyes. Take off the blindfold: look at the facts and choose.
adviceReversed: The tension is growing, and you cannot wait any longer. Make a decision, even an imperfect one.

name: Three of Swords
symbolism: A red heart pierced by three swords floats against grey clouds from which rain is falling. The image is simple and spare, with no figures, as if it concentrated all attention on one feeling.
upright: The Three of Swords speaks of a pain worth acknowledging instead of hiding. It may concern a disappointment, hurtful words or a sense of loss, but it decides nothing final. The rain on the card is also an image of cleansing: tears can bring relief. Naming what hurts is often the first step towards emotional healing.
reversed: The reversed Three may signal that the wound is slowly healing and more calm is returning. Sometimes, though, it points to suppressed sadness that needs a conversation with someone you trust.
reflection: Which pain needs my acknowledgement today?
What helps me to pass through difficult feelings gently?
advice: Acknowledge the pain instead of hiding it. Allow yourself to live through the sadness: it is the first step towards healing.
adviceReversed: The wound is beginning to heal. Let it: stop going back in your thoughts to what hurt.

name: Four of Swords
symbolism: The carved figure of a knight rests on a stone tomb in a church, hands folded in prayer. Above him on the wall hang three swords pointing down, a fourth lies horizontally beneath him, and a stained-glass window shows a scene with figures.
upright: The Four of Swords invites you to stop and rest your mind. After a period of tension, silence is not a waste of time but a way of regaining strength. The card encourages quiet, reflection, or simply a longer break from stimulation. What you put down for a while will be waiting for you.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to difficulty letting go and always staying on alert. It can also signal that the rest is coming to an end and the wish to act is slowly returning.
reflection: When did I last allow myself real rest?
What can I put down for a while in order to regain clarity?
advice: Rest. Before you take the next step you need recovery and quiet: it is not a waste of time.
adviceReversed: Your strength is coming back, and that is good. But do not throw yourself straight into the whirl; return gradually.

name: Five of Swords
symbolism: A man with a slight smile gathers up swords while two figures walk away, hunched, towards the water. Several swords lie on the ground, and ragged clouds streak the sky.
upright: The Five of Swords asks about the price paid for getting your own way. Sometimes winning an argument leaves coldness and distance behind. The card encourages you to reflect on which battles are really worth fighting. Withdrawing need not be a defeat; it can be a wise choice.
reversed: The reversed Five may mean a readiness to make peace or to close an old dispute. It may also point to regret over words that are worth calmly putting right.
reflection: Is there a situation in which winning matters more to me than understanding?
Which dispute could I withdraw from with dignity?
advice: Consider whether this victory is worth its price. Sometimes it is better to let the argument go than to lose the relationship.
adviceReversed: It is time to end the conflict. Hold out your hand, or walk away with dignity.

name: Six of Swords
symbolism: A ferryman pushes a boat along with a pole, and in it sits a cloaked figure with a child beside them. Six swords stand upright in the boat; the water on one side is rough and on the other smooth, and a shore looms on the horizon.
upright: The Six of Swords describes a gradual passage from a harder period towards a calmer one. Not everything is left behind at once; some thoughts travel with you. The card is a reminder that a transition can be quiet and slow and still lead forward. It is worth appreciating the help that lets you keep moving.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to resistance to change, or a feeling that you keep coming back to the same shore. It can encourage you to check what you are still keeping in the boat and what could be left behind.
reflection: What am I slowly moving away from, and where am I heading?
Who or what is helping me through this period?
advice: Move on to calmer waters. Change is needed: leave what is difficult behind you.
adviceReversed: Change is needed, but you are resisting it. Consider what is holding you in place.

name: Seven of Swords
symbolism: A man creeps on tiptoe out of a camp of tents, carrying five swords in his arms. Two more are left stuck in the ground behind him, and he glances over his shoulder with a pleased expression.
upright: The Seven of Swords encourages you to look at where you are acting alone, and by what means. It may be a wise strategy, but also a temptation to dodge a difficult conversation. The card asks about honesty towards others and towards yourself. Sometimes it is worth stopping to consider what you are really taking and what you are leaving behind.
reversed: The reversed Seven may mean a wish to come out of hiding and tell the truth. It may also suggest you are trying to carry too much at once instead of asking for support.
reflection: Where do I choose the shortcut, and what makes me do it?
Is there something I could say openly?
advice: Act cleverly, but honestly. Also check that nobody is playing unfairly with you.
adviceReversed: Something is coming to light. Choose honesty: hiding costs more than it gains.

name: Eight of Swords
symbolism: A woman in a long dress stands blindfolded with her arms loosely bound among eight swords planted in marshy ground. The swords do not close her in a full circle, and a castle rises on a hill in the distance.
upright: The Eight of Swords shows a situation in which the restriction is largely woven out of thoughts. The bonds on the card are loose, and there is space between the swords. The card encourages you to check which beliefs are keeping you stuck. A small movement, a question or a conversation can turn out to be the start of a way out.
reversed: Reversed, the card may mean that the blindfold is starting to slip and you can see more possibilities. Sometimes, though, it points to a fear so strong that it is worth seeking support from someone kind.
reflection: Which belief about myself is keeping me stuck?
What is the smallest movement I could make today?
advice: The cage is mostly in your head. Question the belief that limits you: there is a way out.
adviceReversed: You are beginning to free yourself from fear. Keep going: each step will be easier.

name: Nine of Swords
symbolism: A figure sits up in bed in the dark, face hidden in their hands. Nine swords hang horizontally on the black wall, the quilt is decorated with roses and zodiac signs, and a scene of combat is carved on the side of the bed.
upright: The Nine of Swords describes thoughts that seem bigger at night than by day. Anxiety can be loud, but it does not always tell the truth about reality. The card encourages you to write your worries down, name them and separate the facts from what you imagine. Talking to someone close may bring more relief than you expect.
reversed: The reversed Nine may suggest that the anxiety is beginning to ease and you have more distance. It may also point to worries kept secret, which would benefit from being said out loud.
reflection: Which of my worries is a fact, and which is imagination?
With whom can I share what is giving me no peace?
advice: Your fears are bigger than reality. Share them with someone you trust: by daylight they look different.
adviceReversed: The worst fears are losing their power. Let yourself breathe, and look after your sleep and your peace.

name: Ten of Swords
symbolism: A figure lies face down by calm water, with ten swords stuck in their back and a red cloth thrown over the body. The sky above is dark, but near the horizon it brightens into a golden band of dawn.
upright: The Ten of Swords speaks of the moment when a stage comes to an end and can no longer be kept going. The image is vivid, almost theatrical, as if to stress that it cannot get any worse, so you can begin to get up. The card does not foretell disaster; rather, it encourages you to acknowledge your exhaustion and let go of what has run its course. On the horizon, dawn is already breaking.
reversed: Reversed, the card may mean gradually getting up and regaining strength. It may also point to holding on to something that has already ended, for fear of the emptiness.
reflection: What in my life has already ended, even though I am still keeping it going?
What does my dawn look like after this stage closes?
advice: This is the end of a stage: it will not get any worse. Accept it and start again.
adviceReversed: You are slowly getting back up after a hard time. Do not go back to what hurt you.

name: Page of Swords
symbolism: A young figure stands on uneven, windy high ground holding a sword raised in both hands. Clouds race across the sky, birds circle above, and the figure looks to one side as if listening.
upright: The Page of Swords is the energy of a curious mind that wants to understand and asks questions. The card encourages learning, observing and gathering information before you draw conclusions. It may also point to a rush of new ideas or a wish to speak up. Alertness is valuable when it goes together with openness.
reversed: The reversed Page may mean distraction, hasty words or gossip. It can be a signal to check your sources before you repeat anything.
reflection: What would I like to find out right now?
Am I listening, or just waiting for my turn to speak?
advice: Ask questions and gather information. Stay alert before you make a decision.
adviceReversed: Watch out for gossip and hasty words. Speak less, listen more.

name: Knight of Swords
symbolism: A knight in armour charges at a gallop on a white horse, sword raised high. The trees in the background bend in the wind, and the same violent gust tears at the clouds and the birds.
upright: The Knight of Swords carries a strong impulse to act and to defend your position. Such energy helps to break through stagnation and state your intentions clearly. The card reminds you, though, that speed does not always go hand in hand with good judgement. It is worth checking whether you know where you are rushing to.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to a haste that scatters your strength, or to words spoken too sharply. It may also mean zeal held back that needs a clear goal.
reflection: Where am I rushing to, and is that direction my own?
How can I state my view firmly but without a wounding tone?
advice: Act decisively and quickly: you know clearly what you want. Just do not trample others on the way.
adviceReversed: Haste and sharp words could do harm. Slow down and think before you set off.

name: Queen of Swords
symbolism: The queen sits in profile on a throne decorated with butterflies, holding a sword upright in her right hand. She raises her left hand, open, as if inviting someone or pointing the way, and a single bird flies in the clear sky above her.
upright: The Queen of Swords is a figure who sees clearly and speaks plainly, often because of what she has lived through. The card encourages you to trust your own judgement and to set boundaries without over-explaining. Her insight does not exclude warmth; the open hand shows a readiness to talk. Experience can become a source of wisdom instead of bitterness.
reversed: The reversed Queen may point to coldness used as a shield, or to judging yourself and others too harshly. It can encourage you to combine clarity of thought with gentleness.
reflection: Where do I need to set a clearer boundary?
How can my experiences teach me rather than close me off?
advice: Speak plainly and set boundaries. Insight and independence will help you see the matter clearly.
adviceReversed: Do not be too harsh, on yourself or on others. Honesty does not have to hurt.

name: King of Swords
symbolism: The king sits facing forward on a high throne, holding a sword tilted slightly from the vertical. The back of the throne is decorated with butterflies and crescent moons, and behind him a few trees and two birds can be seen against the clouds.
upright: The King of Swords embodies a mind that weighs arguments and is guided by principles. The card encourages an impartial view of the situation and decisions based on facts. It is the energy of responsible, considered communication. Wisdom appears when logic serves people, not just being right.
reversed: Reversed, the card may mean rigid convictions, or using arguments to dominate others. It may also point to an inner chaos of thoughts that needs putting in order.
reflection: Is my decision based on facts, or on fears?
How can I combine principles with understanding?
advice: Be guided by reason and principle. A cool, objective analysis will give the best result.
adviceReversed: Logic alone is not enough. Take into account the people and the emotions the decision affects.

name: Ace of Pentacles
symbolism: A hand reaches out of a cloud, holding a large gold pentacle inscribed with a five-pointed star. Below it stretches a garden full of white lilies, and a path leads to a gate in a hedge, beyond which mountains rise.
upright: The Ace of Pentacles speaks of the seed of something tangible: a new occupation, a skill or a healthier everyday rhythm. The card encourages you to value what is real and available here and now. Potential becomes something lasting when it is surrounded with patient care. The garden gate is open, but you have to walk through it yourself.
reversed: The reversed Ace may point to an opportunity that has not yet ripened, or to difficulty turning plans into action. It can be a signal to go back to basics and check where you stand.
reflection: Which seed would I like to plant in my everyday life?
What concrete thing can I do to look after my resources?
advice: A concrete opportunity is appearing: seize it. Sow the seed by investing time, work or money in something lasting.
adviceReversed: The opportunity may pass you by. Check that you are planning well before you invest.

name: Two of Pentacles
symbolism: A young man in a tall hat dances while juggling two pentacles joined by a ribbon in the shape of a figure eight lying on its side. Behind him two ships rock on high waves.
upright: The Two of Pentacles shows the art of keeping your balance between different duties. Life can feel like dancing on a shifting wave, and you are learning to move in its rhythm. The card encourages lightness, but also an honest look at how much you can carry at once. Flexibility is a strength as long as it does not leave you breathless.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to too many things in the air and a feeling of overload. It may also encourage you to put one of the balls down and decide what matters most.
reflection: How many things am I trying to keep up in the air at once?
What could I put down to get my lightness back?
advice: You are juggling many things, and you are managing. Stay flexible and set your priorities.
adviceReversed: Too much at once. Give something up before something falls.

name: Three of Pentacles
symbolism: In a Gothic interior a craftsman stands on a bench working on the arch of a vault. Beside him two figures, one in a monk's habit and the other holding an unrolled plan, discuss the progress of the work, and three pentacles are carved into the stone above them.
upright: The Three of Pentacles emphasises the value of cooperation in which everyone contributes their own skill. The card encourages you to share knowledge and to listen to those who see things from a different perspective. Appreciating other people's work and your own builds lasting results. It is a good moment to ask how something could be done better together.
reversed: The reversed Three may signal a lack of coordination in a team, or a feeling that your contribution goes unnoticed. It can encourage a clear conversation about roles and expectations.
reflection: With whom could I build something together?
Do I value my own contribution as much as other people's?
advice: Work together. Your skills combined with other people's will give a solid result: ask for support or an opinion.
adviceReversed: The cooperation is not working out. Agree clearly who is responsible for what.

name: Four of Pentacles
symbolism: A crowned man sits on a stone bench, pressing a pentacle tightly to his chest. Another pentacle rests on his crown, he holds two more down with his feet, and a city spreads out behind him.
upright: The Four of Pentacles speaks of a need for stability and for protecting what you have. Caring about security is natural and important. The card encourages you, though, to check whether you are holding tight to what is precious, or also to what merely takes up space. Sometimes opening your hand gives more peace than clenching it.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to loosening a tight grip and a readiness to share. It may also mean swinging between too much caution and giving away too quickly.
reflection: What am I holding on to out of fear rather than need?
What gives me a sense of security apart from material things?
advice: Secure what you have, but do not clench your fist too hard. Security is not the same as control.
adviceReversed: It is time to open up: share, spend, let go. Holding on tight blocks the flow.

name: Five of Pentacles
symbolism: Two figures trudge through snow on a winter night; one leans on crutches, the other wraps herself in a ragged shawl. They pass a brightly lit stained-glass window showing five pentacles, apparently without noticing it.
upright: The Five of Pentacles describes a period in which you may feel left out in the cold. The card acknowledges the difficulty, but reminds you that the figures are walking together, not alone. The light in the window suggests that support is often closer than it seems. Asking for help is not a weakness but a way of caring for yourself.
reversed: The reversed Five may mean slowly coming out of a hard period and regaining a sense of belonging. It may also point to difficulty accepting support that is available.
reflection: Where can I ask for the support I need?
Who walks beside me in harder moments?
advice: Hard times do not last for ever. Ask for help: support is closer than you think.
adviceReversed: The worst is passing. Accept the help someone is offering you.

name: Six of Pentacles
symbolism: A wealthy merchant holds a pair of scales in one hand and with the other gives coins to one of two kneeling beggars. Six pentacles float above the scene.
upright: The Six of Pentacles speaks of a flow: sometimes you give, sometimes you receive. The card encourages a generosity that does not humiliate, and accepting help without shame. The scales in the merchant's hand are a reminder of fairness and proportion. It is worth considering where in your life the exchange is fair and where it needs adjusting.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to an imbalance, for example giving out of duty, or help that comes with strings attached. It can encourage you to rethink boundaries in relationships built on support.
reflection: Is it easier for me to give or to receive?
Where in my life does the exchange need more balance?
advice: Give and receive in balance. Generosity will come back to you, but do not forget to take as well.
adviceReversed: Check that the exchange is fair. Help with obligations attached may weigh you down.

name: Seven of Pentacles
symbolism: A farmer leans on his hoe and looks at a bush on which seven pentacles have grown among the leaves. His posture expresses tiredness and thoughtfulness, as if he were measuring how much his work has yielded so far.
upright: The Seven of Pentacles is a moment of pausing to look at what has already grown. Growth can be slow and is not always visible from day to day. The card encourages patience and an honest assessment of whether the direction still suits you. Resting in the middle of the work is part of the cultivation.
reversed: The reversed Seven may point to impatience, or a feeling that your effort is not bringing the results you expected. It can be an invitation to change your way of working instead of giving up.
reflection: What has already grown thanks to my work, though I have not noticed it?
Is the direction I am heading in still right for me?
advice: Be patient: the crop is growing. Assess what is working and invest where you can see growth.
adviceReversed: The effort is not paying off. Change the method instead of working even harder in the same way.

name: Eight of Pentacles
symbolism: A craftsman sits at a workbench patiently finishing another pentacle with a chisel. The finished discs hang one above another on a wooden post, one lies at his feet, and the buildings of a town can be seen in the distance.
upright: The Eight of Pentacles describes the joy of improving through repetition and focus. The card values work done carefully, even when nobody happens to be watching. It may encourage you to learn a new skill or deepen one you already have. Mastery grows out of small, everyday steps.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to a perfectionism that takes the pleasure out of work, or to routine without commitment. It can encourage you to remind yourself why you are learning.
reflection: Which skill would I like to develop step by step?
Am I working with commitment, or only out of duty?
advice: Focus on the craft and practise. Steady work and attention to detail will bring results.
adviceReversed: Perfectionism or routine is holding you back. Remind yourself why you are doing it.

name: Nine of Pentacles
symbolism: A woman in a robe decorated with flowers stands in a vineyard full of ripe grapes and nine pentacles. A hooded falcon sits on her gloved hand, and a small snail crawls in the grass at her feet.
upright: The Nine of Pentacles speaks of the satisfaction of what you have built through your own effort and patience. The card encourages you to enjoy a moment of calm and to appreciate your independence. The hooded falcon is a reminder of self-control and the ability to wait. You can allow yourself a little pleasure without having to justify it.
reversed: The reversed Nine may point to a dependence on outside recognition, or to loneliness hidden behind a show of self-sufficiency. It can be an invitation to share your garden with others.
reflection: What that I have built on my own am I proud of?
How can I enjoy what I have without comparing myself?
advice: Enjoy the fruits of your work. You have every right to independence and a little luxury.
adviceReversed: Check that your independence is not loneliness. Let someone come closer.

name: Ten of Pentacles
symbolism: Under an archway sits a grey-haired old man in a rich cloak, stroking two white dogs. Beside him stand a young woman, a man and a child, and the ten pentacles are arranged on the image in the shape of a branching tree; the walls of a household and coats of arms can be seen in the background.
upright: The Ten of Pentacles turns your attention to what lasts longer than a single life: family stories, traditions, values and shared places. The card encourages you to reflect on what you inherit and what you want to pass on. It also speaks of a sense of rootedness and of stability built up over years. Everyday gestures of care become a legacy over time.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to tensions around family expectations, or a feeling that traditions are restricting you. It can encourage you to choose consciously what you want to keep from your inheritance.
reflection: Which values have I received from earlier generations?
What would I like to leave behind for others?
advice: Think long term. Build something lasting, for yourself and for those who will come after you.
adviceReversed: Family or financial matters need putting in order. Do not put off difficult conversations.

name: Page of Pentacles
symbolism: A young figure stands in a green meadow, solemnly holding a pentacle and gazing at it. Behind stretches a ploughed field and a few trees, and the horizon is calm and wide.
upright: The Page of Pentacles is the energy of a student who approaches the world with curiosity and seriousness at the same time. The card encourages learning, experimenting and taking the first steps in something practical. Ideas take shape when you give them attention day after day. You do not have to know how to do everything straight away.
reversed: The reversed Page may point to putting off the start, or a lack of focus despite good intentions. It can be a signal to choose one thing and begin with a small step.
reflection: What practical thing would I like to learn?
What first small step can I take this week?
advice: Learn. A new skill or a practical course will open the way for you: start with the basics.
adviceReversed: Start at last, instead of only planning to learn. A small, regular step is enough.

name: Knight of Pentacles
symbolism: A knight in dark armour sits on a massive horse that stands perfectly still, holding a pentacle before him. A ploughed field stretches behind him, and green sprigs decorate his helmet and the horse's head.
upright: The Knight of Pentacles shows the strength that comes from perseverance and consistency. He is not the fastest, but he reaches his goal step by step. The card encourages you to value a routine that builds things up, and responsibility for the commitments you have made. A slow pace is often the surest way.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to being stuck in a routine that no longer serves you, or to too much caution. It can be an invitation to bring a little freshness into your daily habits.
reflection: Which daily habit truly supports me?
Where does my caution turn into stagnation?
advice: Work steadily and methodically. Slowly but surely you will reach your goal: do not cut corners.
adviceReversed: Too cautious, or too monotonous. Add a little movement and change to the routine.

name: Queen of Pentacles
symbolism: The queen sits on a throne in a garden full of blooming roses, holding a pentacle and looking at it tenderly. The throne is decorated with carved fruit and goats' heads, and a rabbit crouches in the lower corner of the picture.
upright: The Queen of Pentacles embodies warmth combined with practical good sense. The card encourages you to look after your surroundings, your body and your daily rhythm in a way that gives you a sense of being rooted. It speaks of creating a space in which you and others can feel at ease. Caring for yourself matters here as much as caring for your loved ones.
reversed: Reversed, the card may point to neglecting yourself while caring too much for others, or to too strong an attachment to order. It can encourage you to find a balance between giving and resting.
reflection: How can I look after my space and the rhythm of my day today?
Do I care for myself as tenderly as I care for others?
advice: Look after the practical basics: home, health, budget. Care for the concrete things will give you peace.
adviceReversed: You are looking after everyone except yourself. Find time and resources for yourself.

name: King of Pentacles
symbolism: The king sits on a throne decorated with carved bulls' heads, in a robe densely covered with a pattern of vines and grapes. In one hand he holds a sceptre, in the other a pentacle, and the walls of a castle rise behind him.
upright: The King of Pentacles shows a mature stability, built patiently and responsibly. The card encourages you to look with gratitude at what you have managed to create, and to consider how it could serve others too. It is the energy of someone who can create secure conditions for themselves and those around them. True wealth also includes time, relationships and peace.
reversed: The reversed King may point to too much focus on control, or to measuring worth only by possessions. It can be an invitation to remind yourself what the things you are building are for.
reflection: What do I consider my true wealth?
How could what I have built support others?
advice: Go for stability and responsible decisions. Act like someone who is building to last.
adviceReversed: Do not let money or status obscure what matters. Security is not everything.
